title: Laughing and weeping
hookLine: Democritus laughed at the world, Heraclitus wept; Montaigne prefers laughter (Essays 1.50)
last: LOVE THE FRONT; KEEP A ROOM BEHIND IT.

cards: Two philosophers step out of their front doors and look at the same street. The same crowd, the same squabbles, the same people hurrying to things that won't matter by next year. One of them laughs.
The other one cries. Montaigne didn't invent the story; he found it in older writers. What he adds is a vote.
Asked to pick a face for looking at the human race, himself included, he picks one, and his reason isn't about comfort.

teach.b: First, the two faces. In his essay Of Democritus and Heraclitus, Montaigne says Democritus found the human condition vain and ridiculous, and never went out in public without a mocking, laughing face.
Heraclitus, feeling pity for that same condition, went about with a sad face and eyes full of tears. Same world, opposite weather. Second, the vote.
Not, he says, because laughing is more pleasant than weeping, but because it's more disdainful. It condemns us more. It seems to him that we can't be looked down on as much as we deserve.
That's sharper than a cheerful shrug. His laugh has an edge, and he points it at all of us, himself first. Third, the reason underneath.
He doesn't think there's as much misery in us as there is vanity, or as much malice as foolishness. We're not so much wicked as silly; not so much tragic as empty-headed.
Tears take our follies seriously, as if they were grand. A laugh cuts them back to their real size. Fourth, the gentle version.
Today's practice keeps the part that helps: laughing at self-importance, starting with our own.
The email rewritten six times. The grudge over a parking spot. The fear of looking foolish, which is itself a little foolish.
Seen from a step back, a lot of it is comedy.

how: Readers of Montaigne often take this essay as permission to meet human folly, their own first, with a laugh rather than despair, keeping cruelty out of it.

o: the old belief that tears and laughter both heal the body
two philosophers' faces at life; Montaigne chose the laugh
a rule that a wise person should never show any feeling

games.q: Of Democritus and Heraclitus: tap the pairs.

s: Montaigne prefers laughing because it feels nicer than crying
he says it's not because laughing is pleasanter, but because it's more disdainful and condemns us more.
Heraclitus is the philosopher who wept
Montaigne says he felt pity for the human condition and went about with eyes full of tears.
Montaigne thinks people are mostly wicked
he says there's less malice in us than foolishness, less misery than vanity.

games.q: you look out at the human comedy, yourself included, and you have to choose a face. which does Montaigne choose?
o: keep a blank face and say nothing.
games.why: he picks the laugh, and not for comfort: he says it's more disdainful, and we can never be looked down on as much as we deserve.

practice: Pick one thing of your own you've been taking very seriously, not a real grief but something smaller: a worry about what someone thinks, a plan redone too many times, a little rivalry.
Look at it the way Democritus might, from a step up the street: a person, hurrying, very sure this matters. If a smile comes, let it, and keep it kind and pointed at yourself.

wordCard.voice: Laughing and weeping. Democritus laughed at the human condition, Heraclitus wept, and Montaigne chose the laugh, because our trouble is less malice than folly. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: laugh, don't weep. Kept kind, the laugh starts at home. Rest well.
